groups.high: A binding arbitration clause generally directs covered disputes to an arbitral tribunal rather than an ordinary court trial, subject to validity, scope, arbitrability, and mandatory consumer law. It does not automatically waive every substantive statutory right. The UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules provide agreed procedural rules, often for ad hoc arbitration; UNCITRAL itself does not ordinarily administer the dispute. The 2021 version incorporates Expedited Arbitration Rules as an appendix, applicable only with express agreement. Parties can address the seat, governing law, tribunal appointment, language, costs, and procedure. An award is binding, but correction, interpretation, an additional award, limited setting-aside proceedings, and enforcement challenges may exist under the rules and applicable law. Some jurisdictions allow further review, so nonappealability is not absolute worldwide. The New York Convention supports recognition and enforcement subject to its conditions and defenses, not automatic enforcement in every case. Private hearings do not establish blanket confidentiality of all documents and awards; agreements, national law, and transparency rules can change disclosure duties. Arbitration has no ordinary jury, and can offer expertise or procedural flexibility, but is not necessarily cheaper or faster. Unfair consumer terms, inaccessible costs, invalid consent, and class-action provisions need jurisdiction-specific scrutiny. Read the entire clause and obtain advice about enforcement and remaining court remedies rather than assuming the word mandatory defeats all protection.
groups.mid: A binding arbitration clause usually sends covered disputes to arbitrators instead of an ordinary court trial. But the clause must be valid, cover the dispute, and comply with rules on consumer rights and matters that can be arbitrated. It does not cancel every legal right. The UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules set procedures the parties agree to use. UNCITRAL itself does not usually run the case. The 2021 rules include faster, expedited rules, but those need express agreement. The parties can address the legal seat, law, arbitrators, language, costs, and process. An award binds them, but there may be ways to correct it, clarify it, challenge it on limited grounds, or oppose enforcement. Some places allow further review. The New York Convention helps enforce awards, subject to conditions and defenses; enforcement is not automatic. A private hearing also does not make every paper and award confidential. Law, agreement, or transparency rules can require disclosure. Arbitration usually has no jury. It may offer skilled decision makers and flexible steps, but is not always cheaper or faster. Unfair consumer terms, high costs, invalid consent, and class-action terms need checking under local law. Read the whole clause and ask what court remedies remain.
groups.low: A contract may say disputes go to binding arbitration. Arbitrators decide the case instead of an ordinary court trial. But the clause must be valid and cover the dispute. Consumer law and rules on what can be arbitrated still matter. It does not wipe out all your rights. UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules set agreed steps for a case. UNCITRAL itself does not usually run it. The 2021 version includes faster rules, but both sides must expressly agree to use them. The deal can set the legal seat, law, choice of arbitrators, language, costs, and process. The award is binding, but limited ways to correct, clarify, set it aside, or resist enforcement may exist. Further review depends on local law. The New York Convention helps with enforcement, but conditions and defenses still apply. A private hearing does not mean every paper is secret. The law or the agreement may require disclosure. There is usually no jury. The process can offer expertise and flexibility. It is not always faster or cheaper. Unfair terms, costs you cannot afford, lack of valid consent, and class-action limits need advice. Read the whole clause. Ask which court remedies you still have.
groups.source_review: UNCITRAL2021 express-consent expedited rules and procedural framework checked; national consumer enforceability expressly left jurisdiction-dependent.
groups.notes: Corrected inherent total confidentiality, absolute no-review and universal statutory-right waiver assertions.

groups.high: The EU Consumer Rights Directive 2011/83/EU generally gives a 14-day withdrawal right for covered distance and off-premises contracts without stating a reason. For goods, the period normally runs from physical possession by the consumer or their nominated third party; for services, from contract conclusion. Missing required information can extend the period. Withdrawal must be communicated before the deadline by a clear statement; the model form is optional. Goods normally must be returned within 14 days after notice. Traders reimburse within 14 days of notice, including standard outbound delivery costs, but may withhold for goods until receipt or evidence of dispatch, whichever comes first, unless they offered collection. Consumers normally bear direct return costs if properly informed, unless the trader agrees to pay; extra premium delivery costs need not be refunded. Excessive handling can create liability for diminished value, and requested early service performance may require proportionate payment. Exceptions include personalized goods, rapidly perishable goods, certain unsealed hygiene products or recordings/software, specified-date leisure or travel-related services, and fully performed services or started digital content subject to the required consent and acknowledgment. This is not an unconditional zero-cost return for every purchase or every auction. National implementation and any stronger local rights should be checked. Cooling-off is distinct from remedies for faulty goods.
groups.mid: For many EU online, phone, and off-premises purchases, Directive 2011/83/EU gives 14 days to withdraw without a reason. For goods, the clock usually starts when you or your chosen person receives them. For services, it starts when you agree the contract. Missing required information can extend the time. Tell the trader clearly before the deadline. You can use the model form, but do not have to. Return goods within 14 days after giving notice. The trader should refund within 14 days of notice, including standard delivery. For goods, they can usually wait until they get them back or you show proof of sending, whichever comes first. That differs if they offered collection. You normally pay direct return costs if told before purchase, unless the trader agrees to pay. Extra cost for premium delivery need not be refunded. Too much handling may reduce the refund. If you asked a service to start early, payment for the part used may apply. Exceptions include personalized or perishable goods, some unsealed hygiene items, recordings or software, some date-specific travel or leisure services, and completed services or started digital content with the required consent. Check the exact exception and national rules. This is not a free return of everything. Rights for faulty goods are separate.
groups.low: Many EU purchases made online, by phone, or away from a shop have a 14-day right to withdraw. Directive 2011/83/EU gives this right. You need no reason. For goods, time usually starts when you or your chosen person gets them. For services, it starts when the contract is made. Missing required information can give you more time. Tell the seller clearly before the deadline. The model form is optional. Send goods back within 14 days after notice. The seller should refund within 14 days of notice, including standard delivery. They can usually wait for the goods or proof you sent them, whichever comes first. There is a different rule if they offered collection. You normally pay return costs if told in advance, unless the seller agrees to pay. Extra premium-delivery cost need not be refunded. Handling goods too much may reduce their value and your refund. A service you asked to start early may need part payment. Not all purchases qualify. Exceptions include personalized or perishable goods, some opened hygiene items, recordings or software, some dated travel or leisure services, and completed services or started digital content with the required consent. Check the exact terms and local rules. This is not free return of every item. Faulty goods have separate rights.
groups.source_review: EU official withdrawal guidance and Directive9–16 checked for clocks, return/refund costs and exceptions.
groups.notes: Corrected contract/form-receipt clock, universal zero-cost and refund withholding claims.

groups.high: Council Regulation (EU) 2022/1854 was a temporary emergency response to high energy prices, not a general prohibition on excessive prices for all essential consumer goods. Its measures included electricity-demand reduction, a temporary cap on certain electricity producers' market revenues, and a solidarity contribution for relevant petroleum, natural-gas, coal, and refinery businesses. The contribution concerned taxable profits in fiscal years beginning in 2022 and/or 2023 above a 20% increase over the average taxable profits of 2018–2021. That benchmark was not a permitted retail-price increase or a universal price-gouging threshold. The Regulation's temporary measures and subsequent amendments must not be presented as an indefinite general law for every current emergency. Excessive pricing may instead be assessed under applicable national emergency or consumer rules and, for abuse by a dominant undertaking, Article 102 TFEU. A high price alone does not establish all elements of an infringement: market power, the relevant legal standard, costs, context, and evidence matter. Emergency scarcity can make essential demand less responsive and create severe consumer harm, but economic concern must be separated from the legal test. Preserve price records, dates, product details, and the relevant emergency context when raising a complaint with the competent authority. Do not invent a mandatory EU-wide percentage for food, medicines, or all crisis goods from the energy Regulation.
groups.mid: High prices in an emergency can hurt people, but EU Regulation 2022/1854 is not a general ban on price gouging for all essential goods. It was a temporary response to high energy prices. It dealt with lower electricity demand, a cap on some electricity producers' market revenues, and a solidarity contribution from certain oil, gas, coal, and refinery businesses. For that contribution, the profit benchmark was more than 20% above average taxable profits for 2018–2021, for relevant fiscal years starting in 2022 and/or 2023. It was not a limit on retail price rises. The temporary rules must not be treated as a permanent law for all emergencies. Other national emergency or consumer laws may apply. Article 102 TFEU may address excessive prices charged through abuse of a dominant market position. A high price alone does not prove a breach. The law, market power, costs, context, and evidence matter. In a shortage, people may have little choice about buying food, medicine, or fuel. That can make price rises especially harmful. But concern is not the same as proving the legal case. Keep price records, dates, product details, and facts about the emergency. Ask the competent authority which rule applies. Do not use the energy profit benchmark as a universal EU price threshold.
groups.low: A very high emergency price can be harmful. But EU Regulation 2022/1854 is not a general price-gouging ban for all essential goods. It was a temporary energy-price measure. It covered electricity demand, a cap on some producers' revenues, and a solidarity contribution from some oil, gas, coal, and refinery businesses. The contribution used profits more than 20% above the average for 2018–2021. It concerned relevant fiscal years starting in 2022 and/or 2023. This was a profit test, not a cap on shop price rises. Do not treat it as a permanent rule for every crisis. National emergency or consumer laws may apply. Article 102 TFEU can matter if a dominant business abuses its position by excessive pricing. A high price alone does not prove that. Check the rule, market power, costs, facts, and evidence. People may still need food, medicine, and fuel even when prices rise. Shortages can therefore cause real hardship. But a legal claim needs more than concern. Keep receipts, price records, dates, product details, and facts about the emergency. Ask the proper authority which law applies. The energy profit rule is not one price limit for all EU crisis goods.
groups.source_review: Official EU emergency-energy summary checked; dates/profit benchmark distinguished from retail pricing, temporary scope retained.
groups.notes: Replaced false universal anti-price-gouging interpretation with actual energy measures and distinct competition-law context.

groups.high: Food adulteration can involve prohibited harmful substances, fraudulent substitution, or violation of legally required composition, depending on the jurisdiction's definition. It may cause poisoning, infection, chronic organ damage, or economic deception, but not every quality variation has identical criminal elements or health consequences. Examples such as melamine added to milk illustrate potential fraud and toxicity; actual risk requires evidence of the substance, concentration, exposure, and affected product. There is no identified universal WHO Food Safety Protocol that itself creates a worldwide criminal offense with fixed imprisonment, forfeiture, or recall penalties. WHO and FAO provide scientific advice and Codex standards supporting national food control. Binding prohibitions, proof requirements, responsible persons, penalties, and enforcement powers come from applicable national law and other binding instruments. Corporate and individual liability can differ and should not be assumed identical everywhere. Effective controls include traceability, supplier checks, suitable laboratory testing, hygiene, and recall procedures where required. Consumers should avoid suspected unsafe food, retain packaging, batch information and receipts, and report through the relevant food-safety authority. Symptoms or serious exposure require appropriate medical care, not home chemical tests or tasting to verify safety. Distinguish deliberate adulteration from accidental contamination while addressing both under the proper food-safety rules.
groups.mid: Food adulteration can mean adding prohibited harmful substances, replacing an ingredient fraudulently, or breaking legal composition rules. The exact definition depends on the country. It can cause poisoning, infection, long-term harm, or financial loss. But not every quality problem has the same risk or criminal rule. Melamine in milk is an example of possible fraud and toxicity. To assess a real case, experts need to know the substance, amount, exposure, and product. WHO does not have one identified Food Safety Protocol that makes the same crime and penalty apply worldwide. WHO and FAO provide science and Codex standards. National laws set binding offenses, evidence rules, responsibility, penalties, and powers. A company and an individual may have different liability. Do not assume every mistake means prison or forfeiture. Businesses need suitable supplier checks, traceability, testing, hygiene, and recall plans under the rules that apply. If you suspect unsafe food, do not eat it to test it. Keep the pack, batch number, receipt, and other evidence. Report it to the relevant food-safety authority. If someone has symptoms or a serious exposure, seek appropriate medical care. Do not rely on a home chemical test or taste. Deliberate fraud and accidental contamination differ, but both can need action under food-safety law.
groups.low: Food can be unsafe or falsely described. Adulteration may mean a harmful banned substance was added, an ingredient was fraudulently replaced, or legal composition rules were broken. The law in each place defines it. Harm can include poisoning, infection, long-term illness, or loss of money. Not every quality fault has the same risk. Melamine added to milk is one example of possible fraud and toxicity. A real case needs facts about the substance, amount, exposure, and product. There is no identified WHO Food Safety Protocol setting one crime and penalty for the world. WHO and FAO give science and Codex standards. National laws set offenses, proof, liability, penalties, and enforcement powers. Rules for a company and a worker may differ. A mistake does not automatically mean prison or seizure of assets. Businesses need checks on suppliers, records to trace food, suitable tests, hygiene, and recall steps where required. If food may be unsafe, do not taste it to check. Keep the pack, batch number, and receipt. Tell the food-safety authority. If someone has symptoms or a serious exposure, seek proper medical care. Do not rely on a home chemical test. Deliberate fraud and accidental contamination differ, but both may need action.
groups.source_review: WHO/FAO science and national-law relationship checked; no specific country's adulteration penalty asserted without its law.
groups.notes: Removed fabricated WHO worldwide criminal protocol and automatic uniform penalties.

groups.high: Section 60 of Bangladesh's Consumers' Right Protection Act, 2009 requires a complaint about an anti-consumer-right practice to reach the Director General or an empowered Directorate officer within 30 days after the cause of action arises. Its text says a complaint outside that period shall not be accepted. Record the relevant events carefully, but do not assume that every latent-defect or continuing-conduct question has an obvious date without legal advice. Discovery is not an automatic replacement for the statutory trigger, and negotiations should not be assumed to pause the clock. Submit promptly in writing through an accepted channel, with purchase records, seller details, the alleged practice, dates, and supporting evidence; retain proof of submission. The Directorate is the Directorate of National Consumers' Right Protection. Section 61 separately addresses the period for submission of a charge sheet after a complaint; it is not an extension of the consumer's filing period. Civil remedies under Sections 66–67 may be available in appropriate cases, but their procedure, limitation, and prospects require separate advice. Bangladesh's relevant limitation framework is not the UK Limitation Act 1980, and no universal six-year fallback should be promised. Missing the Directorate deadline is serious, but should not be described as automatically deciding every possible remedy under every other law.
groups.mid: Section 60 of Bangladesh's Consumers' Right Protection Act, 2009 sets a 30-day complaint limit. The complaint must reach the Director General or an empowered officer of the Directorate within 30 days after the cause of action arises. The section says a late complaint shall not be accepted. The Directorate is DNCRP, the Directorate of National Consumers' Right Protection. Record what happened and when. If a defect appeared later or the conduct continued, ask for advice about the correct start date. Do not assume discovery always starts a fresh clock. Nor should you assume talks with a seller stop time running. File promptly in writing through an accepted route. Include seller details, purchase records, the alleged practice, dates, and proof. Keep a record of submission. Section 61 deals separately with a charge sheet after the complaint. It does not give you extra time to complain. Sections 66–67 may allow civil remedies in suitable cases. But check the court procedure, time limit, and evidence separately. The UK Limitation Act 1980 is not Bangladesh's law. There is no general promise of a six-year backup period. Missing the DNCRP deadline is serious, but does not by itself settle every possible remedy under another law.
groups.low: Do not wait to complain about a consumer-rights problem in Bangladesh. Section 60 of the Consumers' Right Protection Act, 2009 gives 30 days from when the cause of action arises. The complaint must reach the Director General or an empowered officer of DNCRP. DNCRP is the Directorate of National Consumers' Right Protection. The section says a late complaint shall not be accepted. Keep a clear record of dates and events. A defect found later, or conduct that goes on, may raise a question about the start date. Ask for advice quickly. Finding a fault later does not always give a new 30 days. Talks with the seller may not stop the clock. File in writing through an accepted route. Give the seller's details, proof of purchase, what went wrong, dates, and evidence. Keep proof that you filed. Section 61 is about the later charge sheet. It does not extend your complaint time. Sections 66–67 may offer civil remedies in suitable cases. Those have separate court rules and time issues. The UK Limitation Act 1980 is not the law of Bangladesh. Do not count on a general six-year fallback. A missed DNCRP deadline is serious, but other possible claims need separate advice.
groups.source_review: Authentic English Act Section60 and adjacent61/66–67 checked; no present-day amendment audit beyond published source or individual limitation opinion claimed.
groups.notes: Removed imported UK1980 six-year limitation and categorical cause-date conclusions.

groups.high: Directive 2001/95/EC is the historical EU General Product Safety Directive. Regulation (EU) 2023/988, the General Product Safety Regulation, applies from 13 December 2024 and replaced that directive for the relevant general regime. Product-specific legislation can also matter. Businesses must not treat a dangerous product as merely a quality inconvenience: the responsible economic operator must take the appropriate corrective action, notify competent authorities through the relevant system, and communicate effectively with affected consumers. Action can include bringing a product into compliance, withdrawal from supply, or recall from users, depending on the risk and applicable duties; not every minor defect requires an identical recall. Under the GPSR, identifiable consumers should be directly informed, and recall notices must clearly identify the product, hazard, required action, and remedy without minimizing the risk. Safety-related recall remedies generally offer a choice of at least two among repair, replacement, and adequate refund, subject to the Regulation's conditions and exceptions. Required remedies should be effective, free, and timely. Manufacturers, importers, distributors, and online marketplaces have different roles rather than one identical manufacturer-only duty. Consumers should follow the official notice, stop use where instructed, identify model or batch, and use the stated remedy route. Do not rely on an outdated directive summary as a complete statement of current law.
groups.mid: The old EU product-safety rule was Directive 2001/95/EC. The General Product Safety Regulation, EU 2023/988, replaced it from 13 December 2024 for the relevant general system. Some products also have their own rules. A dangerous product needs proper action, not just a quality excuse. The responsible business must take suitable corrective steps, tell authorities through the relevant system, and inform affected consumers. Steps may include fixing compliance, withdrawing stock, or recalling goods from users. A small defect does not always need the same recall. Under the GPSR, people who can be identified should be contacted directly. A recall notice should clearly state the product, risk, what to do, and remedy. It must not play down the danger. For a safety recall, the remedy generally offers at least two choices from repair, replacement, and adequate refund, subject to the rules and exceptions. Required remedies should work, be free, and be timely. Manufacturers, importers, distributors, and online marketplaces have different duties. If you receive a notice, follow it. Stop using the product if told. Check the model and batch and use the official remedy route. An old directive summary is not a full guide to today's law.
groups.low: A dangerous product may need to be recalled. The old EU general rule was Directive 2001/95/EC. Regulation EU 2023/988 replaced it from 13 December 2024 for the relevant general system. Some products have extra rules. A business must take proper action if a product is dangerous. It must tell the authorities through the right system and inform affected people. Action may mean fixing the issue, taking stock off sale, or asking users to return it. Not every small fault needs the same recall. Under the GPSR, known buyers should be contacted directly. The notice must clearly name the product, explain the risk, and say what to do and what remedy is offered. It must not play down the danger. For a safety recall, people generally get at least two choices from repair, replacement, and an adequate refund. Conditions and exceptions apply. The required remedy should work, be free, and come in time. Makers, importers, sellers, and online marketplaces do not all have identical duties. Follow the official notice. Stop use if it says to. Check your model or batch. Use the official way to claim a remedy. Do not rely only on a summary of the old law.
groups.source_review: Official GPSR applicability/replacement and recall/remedy framework checked; product-specific regime left open.
groups.notes: Updated outdated2001 directive framing; qualified recall triggers and differentiated economic-operator roles.

groups.high: Section 46 of Bangladesh's Consumers' Right Protection Act, 2009 penalizes selling or supplying goods to a consumer in a quantity below the offered weight. The maximum punishment in the published Act is one year's imprisonment, a fine of BDT 50,000, or both. These are statutory ceilings, not an automatic sentence in every case. Section 47 separately addresses a weight or weighing instrument that shows more than the actual weight; it carries the same stated maximum. A substantial-loss threshold should not be invented where Section 46 speaks of less than the offered weight. Compare the promised net quantity and delivered quantity using reliable evidence, keeping packaging, receipts, product details, dates, and the seller's identity. Ordinary packaging weight must not be confused with the quantity of goods promised. Section 60 generally requires a Directorate complaint within 30 days of the cause of action; report promptly rather than assuming informal discussions extend time. Liability and proof must be assessed through the Act's procedures; a discrepancy should not be treated as an automatic conviction without investigation. Other measurement or consumer laws may also apply. The practical aim is truthful quantity and fair payment, with accurate measurement and lawful enforcement rather than relying on the merchant's assurance alone.
groups.mid: Section 46 of Bangladesh's Consumers' Right Protection Act, 2009 covers selling or supplying less than the offered weight. The published Act allows up to one year in prison, a fine of BDT 50,000, or both. These are maximum penalties, not the sentence for every case. Section 47 separately covers a weight or scale that shows more than the actual weight. It has the same maximum. The Act does not say the shortage must be large before Section 46 can matter. Check what net weight was promised and what was actually supplied. Use reliable evidence. Keep the pack, receipt, product details, date, and seller's name. Do not confuse the pack's weight with the amount of goods promised. If you complain to the Directorate, Section 60 generally sets 30 days from the cause of action. Act quickly. Talking to the seller may not extend that time. A discrepancy still needs investigation and proof under the proper process. It is not an automatic conviction. Other measurement or consumer laws may apply too. The aim is honest weight and fair payment, backed by sound checks rather than a seller's word alone.
groups.low: If a seller promises a weight, the goods should match it. Section 46 of Bangladesh's Consumers' Right Protection Act, 2009 covers selling or supplying less than the offered weight. The maximum is one year in prison, a BDT 50,000 fine, or both. This is not the automatic sentence for every case. Section 47 covers a weight or scale that shows too much. It has the same maximum. You do not have to assume only a large shortage matters. Check the promised net weight against the goods supplied. Net weight means the goods, not the pack. Use a reliable check. Keep the pack, receipt, product details, date, and seller's name. These can help prove what was promised and sold. Section 60 generally gives 30 days from the cause of action for a Directorate complaint. Do not wait. Talks with a seller may not give extra time. A short weight still needs a fair investigation and proof. It does not mean the seller is convicted at once. Other measurement or consumer laws may apply. The goal is honest weight for the price you pay, based on good checks rather than only what the seller says.
groups.source_review: Published authentic English Sections46/47/60 checked; no additional current amendment or case-specific conviction claim.
groups.notes: Corrected significant-shortage threshold and automatic sentencing implication.

groups.high: Section 44 of Bangladesh's Consumers' Right Protection Act, 2009 penalizes deceiving a buyer through a false or untrue advertisement for the purpose of selling goods or services. The published maximum is one year's imprisonment, a fine of BDT 200,000 (two lakh taka), or both. The fine is a criminal penalty, not automatically compensation paid to the buyer. Whether an advertisement satisfies the offense requires examining the actual statement, context, evidence, and statutory elements; a broad claim that every negligent omission or ambiguous promotion is automatically criminal goes beyond the section's wording. Retain the advertisement as displayed, including screenshots or recordings, dates, product or service identity, promised features or prices, receipts, and communications showing what was offered. Avoid editing evidence so that context is lost. Directorate complaints generally face Section 60's 30-day period from the cause of action. Civil remedies under Sections 66–67 are distinct from the criminal penalty and can depend on proven loss and the court's decision. Do not promise automatic license revocation, full compensation, or prosecution by a vaguely defined adjudicating officer. Relevant authorities investigate and courts apply the Act's procedures. Truthful marketing and informed consumer choice are the objective; allegations still require proof and lawful process.
groups.mid: Section 44 of Bangladesh's Consumers' Right Protection Act, 2009 covers deceiving a buyer through false or untrue advertising to sell goods or services. The published maximum is one year in prison, a fine of BDT 200,000, or both. That is two lakh taka. It is a maximum, not a fixed sentence. A fine is not automatically money paid to the buyer as compensation. The actual claim, context, evidence, and legal test matter. The section does not say every unclear phrase or negligent omission is automatically a crime. Keep the ad as people saw it. Save screenshots or recordings, dates, product details, promised features or prices, receipts, and messages. Do not cut away context that may matter. Section 60 generally gives 30 days from the cause of action for a complaint to the Directorate. File promptly. Sections 66–67 provide separate civil remedies in suitable cases. Those depend on proof and a court decision; they are not the same as a fine. Do not assume a complaint guarantees license loss, compensation, or a conviction. Authorities investigate and courts follow the Act's process. The aim is truthful marketing, but allegations still need evidence.
groups.low: A seller must not deceive a buyer with a false ad to sell goods or services. Section 44 of Bangladesh's Consumers' Right Protection Act, 2009 covers this. The maximum is one year in prison, a BDT 200,000 fine, or both. BDT 200,000 means two lakh taka. It is not the same sentence in every case. A fine does not automatically go to the buyer as compensation. The claim, context, evidence, and legal test matter. Not every unclear phrase or careless omission is automatically this crime. Keep proof of the ad as shown. Save a screenshot or recording, the date, product details, claims about features or price, receipts, and messages. Keep the full context. Section 60 generally gives 30 days from the cause of action to complain to the Directorate. Do not wait. Sections 66–67 may allow a separate civil claim. A court must decide the remedy on the evidence. It is not the same as a criminal fine. A complaint does not promise a conviction, loss of a license, or payment of all losses. Authorities must investigate and follow the law. The goal is honest advertising and fair consumer choice.
groups.source_review: Authentic English Sections44/60/66–67 checked; penalty distinguished from compensation.
groups.notes: Removed automatically broad negligent/omission liability and guaranteed license/compensation consequences.

groups.high: EU Consumer Rights Directive 2011/83/EU requires clear precontract information about total price or subscription costs, contract duration, and termination conditions for indefinite or automatically extended contracts, along with applicable minimum obligations. It does not itself create a universal rule that every subscription must receive a reminder exactly one month before renewal. National law, sector-specific rules, unfair-contract-term protections, and the particular contract can add duties. An unreasonably early opt-out deadline or hidden renewal clause may raise unfairness issues under Directive 93/13/EEC and its implementation. Distinguish initial withdrawal during the cooling-off period from ending a continuing subscription or preventing renewal: they are not always the same remedy. A withdrawal function under newer online-contract rules is not automatically an unlimited right to cancel any subscription at any time without charge. Review the subscription period, renewal date, notice deadline, charges, cancellation channel, and national or sector rules. Keep the signup terms, billing notices, cancellation request, confirmation, and evidence of unwanted charges. Clear, usable cancellation processes support fair choice, but the exact form, availability, timing, and remedy cannot be invented as a single EU-wide 24/7 rule from the original Directive. If terms or billing appear unlawful, contact the trader and relevant consumer-support body; refund entitlement depends on the facts and law.
groups.mid: Before you subscribe, EU Directive 2011/83/EU requires clear information on price, subscription costs, duration, and how to end an indefinite or automatically extended contract. It also covers relevant minimum commitments. But it does not set one rule that every subscription needs a reminder exactly one month before renewal. National law, sector rules, unfair-term protections, and your contract may add rights. A hidden renewal term or an opt-out deadline set too early may be unfair under Directive 93/13/EEC and local rules. Cooling-off withdrawal is different from ending a running subscription or stopping the next renewal. A newer online withdrawal function is not a promise that every subscription can be cancelled at any time with no cost. Check the term, renewal date, notice deadline, charges, cancellation route, and laws for the country and service. Save signup terms, bills, notices, your cancellation request, and confirmation. A clear, usable way to cancel matters, but the original Directive does not require the same 24/7 button for all subscriptions. If a bill or term seems wrong, contact the trader and a consumer-support body. A refund depends on the facts and the rule that applies, not merely the label auto-renewal.
groups.low: Read the terms before you subscribe. EU Directive 2011/83/EU requires clear facts about price, subscription costs, duration, and how to end an open-ended or automatically extended contract. Minimum commitments matter too. It does not say every service must warn you exactly one month before renewal. Local law, rules for the type of service, and your contract may give more rights. Hidden renewal terms or an opt-out date set too early may be unfair under Directive 93/13/EEC and local law. The first cooling-off right is not the same as ending a subscription later or stopping renewal. A newer online withdrawal tool does not mean all subscriptions can be cancelled at any time for free. Check when the term ends, when it renews, how much notice is needed, charges, and how to cancel. Keep the signup terms, bills, reminders, your request, and any confirmation. Clear cancellation steps matter. But there is no single 24/7 button rule for every subscription in the original Directive. If charges or terms seem wrong, ask the trader and a consumer-support body. A refund depends on the facts and law. Auto-renewal does not settle the issue on its own.
groups.source_review: Directive2011/83 precontract-duration/termination scope checked; no universal one-month reminder inferred; current national/sector specifics not exhaustively audited.
groups.notes: Removed invented one-month pre-renewal reminder and universal24/7 cancellation/refund requirements.

groups.high: GDPR Article 33 requires a controller to notify the competent supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours after becoming aware of a personal-data breach, unless it is unlikely to risk individuals' rights and freedoms. Late notification requires reasons; information may be provided in phases without undue further delay. A processor must notify the controller without undue delay. Awareness is not automatically the first unverified technical alert. Article 34 separately requires clear communication to affected people without undue delay when a breach is likely to create high risk; there is no universal 72-hour consumer-notice deadline. Exceptions include effective protection rendering data unintelligible, later measures ensuring high risk is no longer likely, or disproportionate effort requiring equally effective public communication. Encryption does not automatically remove every risk if keys or other data were compromised. Records must document breaches, effects, and remedial action even where notification is not required. Notices cover nature, relevant numbers where possible, contact details, likely consequences, and mitigation. Articles 33–34 infringements fall within the Article 83(4) tier of up to EUR 10 million or 2% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, while related violations can engage other tiers; a EUR 20 million/4% maximum is not the automatic notification-only category. Risk assessment, containment, and useful protective advice matter alongside timely reporting.
groups.mid: GDPR has two different breach-notice rules. Under Article 33, the controller tells the data-protection authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours after becoming aware of a personal-data breach. There is an exception if risk to people's rights and freedoms is unlikely. If late, explain why. Details can follow in phases without undue further delay. A processor tells the controller without undue delay. The first unverified alert is not always legal awareness of a breach. Article 34 concerns affected people. They must be told without undue delay if high risk is likely. There is no general 72-hour deadline for telling all consumers. Exceptions can apply if strong protection makes data unreadable, later steps remove likely high risk, or direct contact would take disproportionate effort and equally effective public communication is used. Encryption is not enough if keys or other data are exposed. Keep records of every breach, its effects, and what was done, even if no notice is needed. A notice gives the nature, relevant numbers where possible, a contact, likely effects, and protective steps. Articles 33–34 use the Article 83(4) fine tier: up to EUR 10 million or 2% of world annual turnover, whichever is higher. Other related breaches can have different tiers. Assess risk, contain harm, and give useful advice promptly.
groups.low: GDPR has different rules for telling the authority and telling people. Article 33 says the controller must tell the data-protection authority without undue delay. Where feasible, this is within 72 hours after awareness of a personal-data breach. No notice is needed if risk to people's rights and freedoms is unlikely. A late notice needs reasons. More facts can follow in stages without undue further delay. A processor must tell the controller without undue delay. An unverified alert is not always the point when legal awareness starts. Article 34 says to tell affected people without undue delay if high risk is likely. It is not a 72-hour rule for all consumers. Exceptions may apply if data is strongly protected and unreadable, later steps remove likely high risk, or direct contact would be disproportionate and an equally effective public notice is used. Encryption alone is not enough if keys or other data leaked. Record every breach, effects, and action, even if no notice is required. A notice gives the nature, relevant numbers if possible, a contact, likely effects, and protective steps. The fine tier for Articles 33–34 is up to EUR 10 million or 2% of world annual turnover, whichever is higher. Other breaches may have other tiers. Act to assess risk, contain harm, and give useful advice.
